criticism: The reasoning is correct and the issue is critical. The init function is public and has no initializer guard, no onlyOwner restriction, and no check that owner/token are unset. Any external account can call it repeatedly and overwrite owner and token. This grants attacker owner privileges, and with owner-only functions such as withdraw, setHandler, or setSwitch, the attacker can hijack or drain the contract. The only caveat is if deployment/initialization is atomically protected by an external factory or if the snippet is incomplete, but no such guard is shown. Correctness is high, severity is critical, and profitability is high because an unprivileged attacker can take ownership and steal funds.
reason: The init function has no access control and no initialization guard. Any external account can call it at any time to set owner to msg.sender and replace token. Even if the deployer calls init first, an attacker can call init again to overwrite the owner. After becoming owner, the attacker can call setHandler, setSwitch, addLinearVesting, or simply call withdraw to drain all ERC20 tokens held by the contract, including vesting funds.
vulnerability: Public initialization allows anyone to become owner and overwrite token

criticism: The code does use defaultStart rather than schedule.start in its timing calculations. If addLinearVesting indeed records schedule.start = block.timestamp and schedules can be added after defaultStart, then newly added schedules are backdated to the global defaultStart and can release early or fully immediately once releasing is enabled. This can drain pooled vesting funds or underfund other schedules. The reasoning is mostly correct, but the provided snippet does not include addLinearVesting, so correctness depends on that behavior; if a single global start is intended, this may be design rather than a bug. The claim also assumes defaultStart is in the past and that new schedules can be created after it. Severity is high when those conditions hold, but profitability requires the attacker to be a beneficiary or to have the ability to create a schedule, such as through the owner/handler role or the separate init flaw.
reason: addLinearVesting stores a per-schedule start value (block.timestamp), but getReleasableAmount completely ignores schedule.start and instead uses the global defaultStart. If defaultStart is set in the past, any newly added schedule is treated as if it started at defaultStart. A beneficiary of a schedule added after defaultStart can therefore immediately release a large portion or even the full amount once the global switch is open, even though the schedule was just created. This can drain vesting funds much earlier than intended and underfund other schedules.
vulnerability: Backdated vesting due to using global defaultStart instead of schedule.start

criticism: The code confirms that withdraw is onlyOwner and accepts an arbitrary IERC20 without excluding the vesting token. Therefore a malicious or compromised owner can drain the vesting token and any other tokens held by the contract. The reasoning is correct at the code level. However, this is fundamentally an owner privilege/centralization risk rather than an unprivileged vulnerability. The combined attack through the public init function is valid, but that external exploitability is largely inherited from the init flaw. If the owner is trusted, the ability to rescue tokens may be intended. Severity is high when the owner is malicious/compromised or when init is exploitable, but standalone profitability for an arbitrary external attacker is limited unless they can become owner or compromise the owner key.
reason: The withdraw function accepts an arbitrary IERC20 otherToken and does not prevent the owner from withdrawing the contract's vesting token. A malicious or compromised owner can pass the vesting token address and transfer all tokens held by the contract to themselves, including funds reserved for active vesting schedules. Combined with the public init function, an attacker can become owner and immediately use withdraw to steal all ERC20 tokens held by the contract.
vulnerability: Owner can withdraw any token, including the vesting token, draining scheduled funds
